title: High risk-take downs prompting Edmonton police to adjust training
article: Edmonton police are experiencing more high risk-take downs, prompting officers to adjust their training accordingly.

Police Chief Rod Knecht said the city is seeing a huge influx of people, particularly with 18- to 24-year-old males, which studies have shown are more likely to be a victim or perpetrator of violence.

"That's something we have to be aware of. Edmonton is a big city now, it's not a small town anymore and the police have to respond accordingly," said Knecht, noting 15 years ago it was rare to come across a gun when conducting a search or an arrest. Now, it's become a regular occurrence.
"It's more frequent to find a vehicle with a weapon in it and an individual with a weapon on them. That seems to be more consistent."
Knecht's comments come two days after a 24-year-old man was gunned down in a busy residential neighbourhood by members of the police tactical team.

Autopsy results on the victim have yet to be released, but the Sun has learned David Charles Sandaker -- wanted for an April 26 homicide -- was killed around 8:30 p.m. Sunday as police were attempting to place him under arrest near the Brander Gardens townhouses at 51 Street and 149A Avenue.

Shots were fired by both police and Sandaker, who died at the scene -- a paved walking path behind a row of townhouses. An eight-year member of the tactical team was also shot in the leg during the gunplay and taken to hospital with serious, but non life-threatening injuries.

Since the incident is being investigated by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), Knecht said he is limited with what he can say, but noted police had started surveillance on the victim -- wanted for second-degree murder -- and had followed him for a period of time.

"There was an opportunity to effect an arrest based on an outstanding warrant and when we went to effect that arrest obviously...all hell broke loose," said Knecht, noting the man was not a resident of the area. Officers were well aware he was dangerous and could be armed, which is why tactical members were brought to the scene.

"I know residents were concerned. We tried to take him down in an area where houses weren't in the immediate -- unfortunately that's not what happened and it's a tragic circumstance. But the public need not be concerned. These don't happen very often. Unfortunately it did happen and it was somewhat out of our control -- the unpredictability of an individual wanted on a homicide warrant."
The wounded officer underwent surgery Monday morning. Knecht said the operation was relatively successful, but there were some complications, which is why the officer remains in hospital.
